claims.text: Combining in situ aberration-corrected STEM heating with molecular dynamics simulations can investigate nanoparticle thermal behavior at atomic scale.
This combined method can reveal the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles is size-dependent.
The thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles includes diffusion-driven phase transitions.
Pulsed laser deposition can be used to synthesize the FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles for this study.
A SiN membrane is a suitable support for the proposed FeCuCrCoNi heating experiment.
A heating range from approximately 298 K to 973 K is suitable for examining the target nanoparticles.
The experiment is to be performed under high-vacuum conditions.
Increasing temperature activates pronounced atomic diffusion in quinary high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Thermally activated atomic diffusion can drive surface phase separation and formation of a segregated surface layer.
Surface-to-volume-ratio differences cause diffusion and surface phase separation to vary with nanoparticle size.
Thermally induced diffusion and structural rearrangements are more pronounced in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles because they have a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo structural changes at lower temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
Reducing FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle size lowers thermal stability.
Substrate interactions or deviations in composition could modify the proposed size-dependent behavior.
Failure to observe a statistically significant size dependence in onset temperature or diffusion-driven structural change would falsify the hypothesis.
A contradiction between experimental structural evolution and the sequence predicted by molecular dynamics would falsify the proposed mechanism.
